# Kururin Squash!

Kururin Squash! (Japanese: くるりんスカッシュ！; Hepburn: Kururin Sukasshu!) is a 2004 action video game developed by Eighting and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo GameCube. It is the third title in the Kururin series, following the Game Boy Advance games Kuru Kuru Kururin (2001) and Kururin Paradise (2003), and the first entry on a home console. The game was released in Japan on October 14, 2004 and is officially styled with an exclamation mark. It adds attack-capable “Helirin” variants, boss encounters, local multiplayer for up to four players, and Game Boy Advance link cable features to the series’ core “rotating craft through narrow courses” concept. 

## Gameplay

Kururin Squash! builds on the series’ central idea of piloting a perpetually rotating craft (the Helirin) through maze-like stages while avoiding contact with walls and obstacles. The GameCube entry presents the action with 3D graphics and an over-the-shoulder/angled camera, while keeping the precise collision-avoidance and route-learning that define the series. The GameCube controller’s analog stick is used for movement, with button inputs assigned to actions on certain Helirin variants. 

Distinctive mechanics introduced in this installment include multiple “action Helirin” forms that can attack or traverse hazards in new ways. Official materials and contemporary coverage describe variants that can punch, emit flame, and submerge to pass underwater obstacles; these forms are leveraged in new stage types, including one-on-one boss battles and competitive multiplayer modes. The official site also details an action-learning system with training modules tied to specific areas, introducing actions under controlled conditions before they appear in main stages. 

Modes and features presented on the official site and in press coverage include:
- Story-style progression with boss encounters built around the new action Helirin mechanics. 
- Time Attack, with leaderboard-oriented stage completions. 
- Versus modes for up to four players on split-screen (racing and battle-style competition). 
- Game Boy Advance link cable connectivity (GBA–GameCube), noted on the product page’s specifications. 

Contemporary import coverage from IGN further notes course elements such as springs that alter rotation and special Helirin forms used for attacks and rail-riding, and summarizes the multiplayer as split-screen up to four players. 

## Narrative and presentation

The game conveys a light narrative through short sequences between stages, while keeping its focus on mechanics. Eurogamer’s review characterizes Kururin Squash! as “built around guiding a perpetually spinning stick through maze-like courses” and observes that the 3D backgrounds and “bizarre” story interludes are aesthetically charming but not central to play. 

Visually, the title uses colorful 3D environments and varied stage motifs aligned to each Helirin action type. Audio was composed by Atsuhiro Motoyama (本山淳弘), credited as the game’s composer. 

## Development

Kururin Squash! was developed by Eighting Co., Ltd. and published by Nintendo. The official developer page highlights the shift to GameCube and analog controls, along with the introduction of action-capable Helirin forms, boss characters, and four-player battles. 

Staff credits captured from the game’s end credits include:
- Producers: 佐藤 浩; 豊嶋 真人
- Production supervision: 波多野 信治; 藤澤 知徳
- Planning: 弓削 雅稔; 永山 尊嗣
- Story: 横尾 憲一
- Main program: 渡辺 康成
- Program lead: 落合 雄一
- Programmers: 西田 一郎; 杉田 克弘; 竹井 淳
- Graphic lead: 辰田 光章
- Graphics: 横尾 憲一; 米井 ゆき; 久保田 真野; 池北 久志; 日髙 美智子; 尾崎 徹
- Course production: 弓削 雅稔; 永山 尊嗣; 池北 久志
- Character design: 小田部 羊一; 横尾 憲一; 久保田 真野; 池田 善高
- Music: 本山 淳弘
- Coordination: 廣瀬 美由貴; 鈴木 隆之助
- Testing support: 任天堂スーパーマリオクラブ 

The official announcement on GAME Watch (Impress) sets the context of the GameCube version as the series’ third entry and the first on a home console, outlining the design goal to expand “action” elements with attack-capable Helirin and to diversify modes with boss fights and four-player battle and race options. 

No official disclosures on engine or proprietary tools were published on the pages consulted. 

## Release and distribution

- Platform: Nintendo GameCube (product code DOL-P-GKQJ). 
- Publisher and developer: Nintendo; Eighting. 
- Japan release date: October 14, 2004. 
- Price: 3,619 yen before tax on Nintendo’s product page; contemporary press lists 3,800 yen, consistent with tax-inclusive pricing at the time. 
- Genre and players: Action; 1–4 players (local). 
- Memory card blocks: 4. 
- Peripherals: Game Boy Advance link cable supported. 
- Barcode: 4902370509601. 

Nintendo’s Japanese product site served as the game’s official web hub, with sections for “About,” “Versus,” “Boss,” “Time Attack,” connectivity with Game Boy Advance, and “special hints.” The title was announced and previewed in Japanese media (GAME Watch) on September 22, 2004, and appeared in IGN’s “Gaming Life in Japan” and “Now Playing in Japan” columns ahead of release, which summarized the premise and listed its budget price point. 

An official guidebook was published by Shogakukan as a “Nintendo Official Guidebook” (Wonder Life Special), covering characters, modes, controls, and complete stage maps for the “adventure” and “challenge” modes; retailer listings confirm the volume’s release on November 12, 2004. 

No ports, reissues, or releases in regions outside Japan have been announced on the consulted official and professional media pages. 

## Reception

Contemporary Japanese coverage introduced the game’s new mechanics and modes, emphasizing the addition of attack-capable Helirin, boss battles, and four-player versus play. 

Eurogamer’s review offered a qualified assessment: it praised the underlying concept and variety in stage types (including submarine sections, projectile waves, destructible block puzzles, and a flamethrower segment), while arguing that the main puzzle mode was comparatively undemanding and recommending the earlier Game Boy Advance entries over the GameCube installment for sustained challenge. The review also remarked that the 3D presentation and story scenes were pleasant but nonessential to the gameplay loop. 

In import coverage, IGN highlighted Kururin Squash! as a budget-priced GameCube release in Japan, summarizing its rotating-navigation mechanics, special Helirin forms, and four-player split-screen multiplayer. 

Public weekly sales charts published by Inside Games (reporting Media Create data) for October 10–17 and October 25–31, 2004, did not list Kururin Squash! among their respective top-ten software rankings, which were dominated by Game Boy Advance and PlayStation 2 titles and (later in October) Mario Tennis GC on GameCube. These charts provide market context around the week of the game’s release. 

## Legacy and impact

Kururin Squash! is frequently cited in import and retrospective discussions as the series’ 3D evolution on GameCube, retaining the precise collision-avoidance core while expanding with action-oriented Helirin variants and party modes. In later retrospectives, Hookshot Media’s Nintendo Life featured the game among “overlooked GameCube gems,” describing it as an effective extension of Kuru Kuru Kururin’s design on home console. 

Eighting’s official catalog lists Kururin Squash! alongside the broader Kururin series, reflecting the developer’s continued association with the brand. Although no re-releases have been announced, the title remains referenced in import features and databases that catalog Japan-only GameCube releases.

2.content: ![Image 1: 「くるりんスカッシュ！」とは？](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/about/b11.gif)![Image 2: A 360x40 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/about/b12.gif)![Image 3: A 20x40 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/about/b13.gif) ゆっくりくるくるまわる特殊ヘリコプター「**ヘリリン**」を操作して壁や障害物、敵などにぶつからないようにゴールまで進めていくゲームなんだ。![Image 4: A 10x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/spacer.gif) ![Image 5: A 10x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/spacer.gif)![Image 6: クルリン＆ヘリリン](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/about/heririn01.gif)![Image 7: ゲーム画面](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/about/ss01.jpg)![Image 8: A 10x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/spacer.gif) これまでは普通のヘリリンしかなかったんだけど、**うさぎ先生**が新しく色んな機能を持った**アクションヘリリン**を作ったんだって。 アクションヘリリンを使えば障害物や敵を壊して進めるからスカッと爽快だよ！ ![Image 9: A 20x120 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/about/b14.gif)![Image 10: アクションヘリリン](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/about/heririn02.gif)![Image 11: A 20x120 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/about/b15.gif) ![Image 12: アクションヘリリン](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/about/heririn03.gif) ![Image 13: ==========](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/bar.gif) ![Image 14: くるくるくるりん](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/about/b_soft01.jpg)ゲームボーイアドバンスソフト [「くるくるくるりん」へ](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/n08/akrj/index.html)![Image 15: くるりんパラダイス](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/about/b_soft02.jpg)ゲームボーイアドバンスソフト [「くるりんパラダイス」へ](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/n08/a9qj/index.html)

任天堂、GC「くるりんスカッシュ!」 攻撃可能なヘリリン追加でゲームモードも多彩に! ------------------------------------------- [![Image 11: Gamecube cover art for Kuru Kuru Kururin Squash features a light blue airplane contraption, cartoonish clouds, rainbow arches, and the game's logo in bright yellow letters](https://game.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/20040922/kururi01.gif)](https://game.watch.impress.co.jp/docs/20040922/kururi01.htm) **10月14日 発売予定** **価格：3,800円** 任天堂株式会社は、ニンテンドーゲームキューブ用アクション「くるりんスカッシュ!」を10月14日に発売する。価格は3,800円。 GC用「くるりんスカッシュ!」は、2001年発売のゲームボーイアドバンス用「くるくるくるりん」、2003年発売の同じくGBA用「くるりんパラダイス」に続く、シリーズ3作目の本作で初のGC用作品となる。ゆっくりと回転する特殊なヘリコプター「ヘリリン」を操作し、壁や障害物を避けながらゴールを目指す。多彩なコースにさまざまな仕掛けが用意されており、アクションゲームとしながらもパズル的な要素も強い。 これまでのシリーズ作品では、ただ障害物を避けるだけだったが、今作ではアクションが可能なヘリリンも登場する。パンチや炎で敵を倒したり、水中にもぐって障害物をやり過ごすといった特殊操作が可能で、攻略のバリエーションを広げるとともに、アクション性や爽快感を高めている。 このアクション機能を活用し、ボスとの1対1での対決ステージや、プレーヤー4人で対戦できる「バトル」なども新たに追加されている。 | 3.title: アクションヘリリンでスカッと攻撃！
3.content: ![Image 1: A 580x40 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka01.gif) ![Image 2: A 20x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/spacer.gif)**アクションヘリリン**は、うさぎ先生が作った新しいヘリリンなんだ。 それぞれ特別な機能を持っていて、特定のステージでは、**Ａボタンでさまざまなアクションを行うことができる**んだよ！![Image 3: A 20x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/spacer.gif) ![Image 4: A 20x20 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka02.gif)![Image 5: A 20x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/spacer.gif)![Image 6: A 20x20 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka03.gif) ![Image 7: ヘリボカーン](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka11.gif) ![Image 8: A 20x118 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/heri11.gif)![Image 9: ヘリボカーン](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/heri12.gif) ![Image 10: ゲーム画面](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ss01.jpg)![Image 11: A 20x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/spacer.gif)ヘリボカーンは、**スウィートアイランド**で使えるよ。Ａボタンを押すとヘリリンの翼からパンチが出るんだ。敵に当てると倒すことができるし、岩に当てると壊すことができるんだって。![Image 12: A 20x68 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka13.gif) ![Image 13: ムービーを見る！](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/b_movie01.jpg) ![Image 14: うさぎ先生：近接攻撃用ヘリリン。もともとは、高い木になっているリンゴを収穫するために設計したんだけど、クルリンがピンチになりそうだったから攻撃用に改造したんだ。](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/usa01.gif) ![Image 15: A 20x20 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka14.gif)![Image 16: A 20x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/spacer.gif)![Image 17: A 20x20 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka16.gif) ![Image 18: ヘリバシャーン](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka21.gif) ![Image 19: A 20x68 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka22.gif)ヘリバシャーンは**ナチュラルワールド**で使えるよ。Ａボタンを押すと水中にもぐり、はなすと浮き上がるんだ。Ａボタンを押し続けると、一定時間もぐることができるよ。![Image 20: ヘリバシャーン](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/heri21.gif)![Image 21: ヘリバシャーン](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/heri22.gif) ![Image 22: ゲーム画面](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ss02.jpg)![Image 23: ヘリバシャーン](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/heri23.gif) ![Image 24: ムービーを見る！](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/b_movie02.jpg) ![Image 25: うさぎ先生：水上用ヘリリン。海水浴用に作られていたレジャー用のヘリリンがもとになっているんだ。ふだんは水の上に浮いているけど、操縦席に水を入れるともぐることもできるよ。でも、クルリンの息がつまりそうになったら、自動的に浮上するぞ！](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/usa02.jpg) ![Image 26: A 20x20 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka24.gif)![Image 27: A 20x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/spacer.gif)![Image 28: A 20x20 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka26.gif) ![Image 29: ヘリボーボ](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka31.gif) ![Image 30: ヘリボーボ](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/heri31.gif)![Image 31: ゲーム画面](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ss03.jpg) ![Image 32: ヘリボーボ](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/heri32.gif)![Image 33: A 20x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/spacer.gif)ヘリボーボは**スノースケープ**で使えるよ。Ａボタンを押し続けると炎を出すよ。また、Ｂボタンを押しながらＡボタンを押すと、炎が長くなるんだ。![Image 34: A 20x68 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka33.gif) ![Image 35: ムービーを見る！](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/b_movie03.jpg) ![Image 36: うさぎ先生：火炎放射ヘリリン。クルリンが寒い地方に行くっていうから作ってみたんだ。スピードを出してエンジンの出力を上げると、炎も長くのびるようになる。オーバーヒートの心配もないんだよ！](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/usa03.gif) ![Image 37: A 20x20 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka34.gif)![Image 38: A 20x1 image, likely be a tacker probe](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/spacer.gif)![Image 39: A 20x20 small image, likely a logo, icon or avatar](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka36.gif) ![Image 40: ヘリブルーン](https://www.nintendo.co.jp/ngc/gkqj/aheri/ka41.gif) ![Image 41: A 20x88 small image, likely a logo, icon 10.content:
Are you a big import gamer? Did you shout out an orgasmic cheer when you first touched the impressive _Mawaru Made in Wario_ Japanese packaging? Then you've followed the right link!This weekly section on IGN will keep you up to date on what games were released over the previous week in Japan. If you want to keep informed of the import scene, be sure and check back once-again-every week.

The following games were released between 10.11.04 and 10.17.04. Click on the name to see all of IGN's current coverage on the title.

**PLAYSTATION 2**

**[Hitman: Contract](https://ps2.ign.com/objects/566/566995.html)**  
**Publisher: Eidos  
Genre: Hard Boiled, Action, Adventure; Release: 10.14.04  
Price: 6090 yen, Memory: 500K  
**This game is already out in America, so we don't feel too compelled to write anything about it in this space. Instead, we're going to take up space with the following whimsical anecdote. _Hitman: Contract_ is actually arriving to Japan before _Hitman: Silent Assassin_. Ahh, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha. Isn't that anecdote whimsical? Ahh, ha, ha, ha, ha, ha.

**[Burnout 3: Takedown](https://ps2.ign.com/objects/640/640596.html)**  
**Publisher: Electronic Arts  
Genre: Race, Action; Release: 10.14.04  
Price: 7140 yen, Memory: 81K  
Other: Compatible with Network Adapter, GT Force and GT Force Pro  
**Two games into this week's software list and we already have two American, and therefore inferior, games. Ha, ha, ha... just kidding. _Burnout 3_ rawks, especially on the PS2 which, being the best selling system in the world, is obviously the most superior system. Ha, ha, ha... just kidding. Actually, EA released only the PS2 version of _Burnout 3_ in Japan, and got lots of favorable reviews for it. Will it actually sell? Are you hardcore enough to buy the Japanese version just for the packaging? Are you answering these questions aloud?

**[Kappa no Kaikata - How to breed Kappas](https://ps2.ign.com/objects/707/707199.html)**  
**Publisher: Konami  
Genre: Comic, Raising, Adventure; Release: 10.14.04  
Price:7140 yen, Memory: 138K  
**This unexpected Konami game places you in the role of Hiroshi, who's forced to spend his summer at his grandparent's house. Hiroshi's grandparents have these green, prank-prone creatures called Kappas, and you earn your keep by raising them -- teaching them manners, guiding them and so-forth. The game includes over thirty manners which can be taught to the Kappas. As you play, you'll take part in Kappa versus Kappa sumo fights and try out mini games that are set up similar to _Dance Dance_.

**[Simple 2000 Series Vol. 64: The Splatter Action](https://ps2.ign.com/objects/707/707734.html)**  
**Publisher: D3 Publisher  
Genre: Horror, Action; Release: 10.14.04  
Price: 2100 yen, Memory: 70K  
**In this latest _Simple 2000_ series game, you play as a scarecrow who must defeat baddies in order to avenge his parents who were injured when the evil Jagado took over the world. You can make use of your bare hands, punching and kicking your way past creatures of the night, or switch to a chainsaw mode and use something a bit stronger against your enemies. Don't use the chainsaw too much, though, as its gas supply slowly depletes. Collect coins by defeating enemies in order to purchase recovery and special action items from a shop that appears at the start of each of the game's seven stages.

**[Simple 2000 Series Vol. 65: The Kyonshi Panic](https://ps2.ign.com/objects/707/707735.html)**  
**Publisher: D3 Publisher  
Genre: SF, Action; Release: 10.14.04  
Price: 2100 yen, Memory: 200K  
**This rescue game takes place years in the future in a Shanghai that's been overrun with demons called Kyonshis. You play as a demon-fighting special forces team member who must protect people from Kyonshi attack as you attempt to evacuate a building. Use swords, guns, and even barriers made of rice (no kidding!) to weaken the Kyonshis, then stab them with your lucky charm. The people you're trying to protect all have unique traits, some being slow, others being weak, and you'll have to study their data in order to properly guide them to safety. You can send commands to the people you're guiding, telling them when to stop and when to play dead (this latter act makes the Kyonshis stop their attack).

**[Meshimase Romanchabou](https://ps2.ign.com/objects/703/703012.html)**  
**Publisher: D3 Publisher  
Genre: Love, Management, Simulation; Release: 10.14.04  
Price: 5040 yen, Memory: 435K  
**D3 gives the world just what it wanted: another reverse love simulation. In this game, you play as Chitoze, the daughter of a family who owns a cake shop. In order to make an impressive appearance in an upcoming cake-off, you've been placed in charge of your store for a one year period. Tt's there that you meet five hunky cake-cooking menz. This game is like your typical love simulation, with lots of loosely-interactive conversation sequences where you selections help to increase or decrease the feelings the boys have for you. You also have to create a work schedule for everyone in the store, taking into account rest periods and money. Random events get you into close quarters with some of the guys.

**[Daidassou: The Great Escape](https://ps2.ign.com/objects/489/489881.html)**  
**Publisher: Marvelous Interactive  
Genre: Movie, Action; Release: 10.14.04  
Price: 7329 yen, Memory: 315K  
**The original movie was great, but the game made IGNPS2 comment, "Should you be planning your own escape?" Ha, ha, ha... Kaiser, you so funny! Pick up this import if you ever had to dig a tunnel in order to flee from prison.

**GAMECUBE**

**[Kururin Squash](https://cube.ign.com/objects/696/696537.html)**  
**Publisher: [Nintendo](https://games.ign.com/objects/025/025047.html)  
Genre: Comical, Action; Release: 10.14.04  
Price: 3800 yen  
**This game follows up on the two Game Boy Advance _Kururin_ titles, with Nintendo acting as publisher this time around. You play as Kururin, who boards a helicopter in order to find his family. As you spin through levels, you must make sure to avoid making direct contact with any walls or objects. The level designs require that you know when to speed up and slow down movement and rotation, and when to bump into springs in order to change your direction of rotation. Kururin also has special versions of his helicopter which can be used to punch enemies and soar through a stage on a rail. Split screen play for up to four is included as well.

**GAME BOY ADVANCE**

**[Mawaru: Made in Wario](https://gameboy.ign.com/objects/695/695223.html)**  
**Publisher: Nintendo  
Genre: Variety, Action; Release: 10.14.04  
Price: 4800 yen; Includes backup feature  
Other: Rotation Sensor and Rumble feature built into cartridge.  
**The first _Made in Wario_ introduced the world to a gaming concept so wild and fun, it made people laugh aloud. The second _Made in Wario_ game took that idea and made it into a wild multiplayer experience. For the third game, Nintendo has taken things even further by building a rotation sensor and rumble feature into the cartridge. Most of the mini games require that you rotate the Game Boy Advance unit (not rotate yourself, as the game clearly warns before you start playing). Over 200 games split into 15 genres, including a collection of classic NES titles, have made the cut into this latest Nintendo masterpiece.

**XBOX**

**[Hitman: Contract](https://xbox.ign.com/objects/566/566982.html)**  
**Publisher: Eidos  
Genre: Hard Boiled, Action, Adventure; Release: 10.14.04  
Price: 6090 yen; Memory: 32 Blocks  
**Eidos is the only publisher still giving full Japanese releases to Xbox games.

That does it for this week's list. Remember, if you want to keep ahead of the Japanese game scene, be sure and check out our weekly Gaming Life in Japan article. In addition to the week in review, the latest charts, an up-to-date release schedule and a letters section, the latest issue features a look at the _Viewtiful Joe_ cartoon, scans from the Square Enix TGS booklet and Makiko Kawajima as the latest young idol. Check out the latest issue [by browsing here](https://insider.ign.com/articles/556/556080p1.html).

Ah, this takes us back. School fetes, manoeuvring rings around twisty wire mazes without sounding a buzzer, perspiration accumulating in the furrows of our infant brow as we overcome the trickiest sections, and the eventual consolation of an "Aw, so close!" when our trademark steadiness eventually fails us and the buzzer cruelly sounds. We'd swear blind they magnetised bits of the wire to save on the lollypop prize budget. But we still wanted another go.

Kururin, in its various forms, is not much more than an update of that buzz bar idea. The goal is to direct a perpetually spinning stick around mazes using the analogue control without touching the sides or any of the course obstacles more than twice. With only a few health-replenishing spinny flower icons dotted throughout each level, and only the option to vary the speed of the stick-spin using the right shoulder button, any gamer can easily imagine how it challenges and how it locks you in with its charming simplicity.

Sticky situations
-----------------

![Image 1](https://www.eurogamer.net/1_p6HTjI1.jpg)

As it's grown from this simple template across three instalments (the first of which, Kuru Kuru Kururin, was among the first wave of Western GBA titles), Kururin has introduced other goals and quirks to the reaction-driven template. You also have to think about collecting 100 per cent of any given level's coins, spread around the play area and sometimes off the beaten track in side areas that involve risk as well as reward, and as we arrive at this Cube instalment, we discover that Nintendo's chosen developer Eighting has managed to expand the idea without separating it entirely from its charm, introducing variations like submersible craft, guns, boxing gloves, on-rails flamethrowing and even whirlwind-chucking and boss battles.

Playing it on anything larger than a 14" television is glorious overkill. The inescapable truth is that it would work just as well played on a Casio watch screen as long as the stick and the walls were distinct; the 3D backgrounds and bizarre, typically Japanese story sequences featuring our ducky hero and his hazard-prone adversaries are charming but totally unnecessary. And that's just as well, because sadly these new levels aren't as pure and addictive as straightforward Kururin puzzling, and as a result we'd recommend the series' previous offerings over this one, even if it were not because of Eighting's attempts to grow the formula.

But that's not to say that Kururin Squash is a bad example of a Kururin game by any stretch. The main puzzle mode, which features some 40 or so levels, never asks you to do more than get to the end without hitting the sides too much, even if it varies the manner in which you achieve this and likes to tease you with tricky-to-obtain loot whose precarious positioning threatens to undo the last few minutes worth of effort, and overall we had no qualms about sitting in front of this for several hours non-stop, just as we did with previous Kururin.

Duck and cover
--------------

![Image 2](https://www.eurogamer.net/2_wEo2Kx1.jpg)

Another option is a sort of 'race' mode where the challenge is not to collect loot and hitting the barriers is not such a worry, but instead the goal is to navigate similar but distinctly simpler Kururin mazes and hit the goal within the target time. To make things a bit less frustrating, these levels are also split up by regular checkpoints, to which you'll return if you take just two hits in any given section.

There's also a multiplayer mode that supports this manner of racing for up to four players in split-screen, which can be manic when your sticks are clanging together, and finally there's a deathmatch-ish mode, which treats the game's new abilities like the flamethrower and boxing gloves as short-burst power-ups in a competitive mode reminiscent of [Super Monkey Ball](https://www.eurogamer.net/games/super-monkey-ball)'s Monkey Target, where the goal is to finish up with the most coins by grabbing any that are strewn about and mashing your friends to mug them of their accumulated wealth.

Returning though to the leading light of the piece, the puzzle mode, it's pleasing to note that the level design can be as inventive as ever. Basic puzzle levels, featuring nothing more than a rotating stick, are definitely the most satisfying, as you strain to manoeuvre the spinning stick around tightly constructed mazes without incurring damage, using bounce pads to change the spin direction and avoid touching the sides, and dodging block-crushers and other moving obstacles at the same time. At its absolute best you'll be changing spin direction fluidly as you navigate tight, impossibly twisty pathways, and you'll emerge with a huge grin on your face. But, to be fair, the variations have their moments too. The submarine in particular, which brings with it the ability to dive underwater for a spell (the "water meter" in this case being the sight of the little ducky's icon in the bottom left gradually filling up with water as he pants and cries out) adds obvious depth, exploited by Eighting with mines and coins on the surface as well as underwater, various other surface obstacles like logs and a mixture of rapids and whirlpools to propel them - and you - around in a manner that demands more of your eager thumbs than regular levels.

Billed prominently
------------------

![Image 3](https://www.eurogamer.net/3_S9c35Rd.jpg)

Boxing gloves, meanwhile, allow you to smash up enemies (the more challenging of which herald some coinage and do not respawn), while the projectile-firing effort has you doing similar but with steadier streams of enemies to dodge (including ChuChu Rocket-style trains of what we think are mice, and, at its best, huge caterpillars barrelling after you like that rock in Raiders of the [Lost Ark](https://www.eurogamer.net/games/lost-ark)), and introduces mazes of green red blocks that bar the way and have to be excised by hunting down the destructible green blob which then blows the rest up along with any circling enemies in a flashy chain reaction. Hitting things with your projectiles is all the more difficult when you can't stop spinning, of course.

Then there are the whirlwind levels, which are some of the most traditionally puzzle-like, allowing you to charge up twisters by holding A and then unleash them in a chosen direction to strike at enemies, block off streams of fire, blow cloud cover out of the way, and spin large propellers that bar your progress; doing so also involves judging whether or not the movement of the blades will uncork flamethrowers that you can't dodge, and planning against such an eventuality.

Apart from one final spinny alternative, flamethrowing's the only other thing - and interestingly it's on rails, the idea being to spit flame (a beautiful effect, incidentally) by holding A and using the analogue stick to twist your chopper blade as you see fit to dodge track-side obstacles and enemies. You can speed up movement by holding B, which also extends reach of the fire, and Eighting often keeps you moving faster than you can really cope or pursues you with big enemies who take some whittling down before they die and will catch up unless you keep them at arm's length by using B to set a solid pace.

Boss design, finally, plays on each of these themes one by one. The first boss, for example, sits in the middle of the screen rotating his surroundings (including obstacles that you have to dodge), and you have to whack things with your boxing glove so they tumble into his command console and kill him off. In a sense, it's not just one good puzzle game idea, but a group of them built around a simple, almost faultlessly executed premise.

Increasingly fowl?
------------------

![Image 4](https://www.eurogamer.net/4_OmaElFs.jpg)

Or it would be, if it weren't for the fact that it isn't faultlessly executed at all. Heading into the main puzzle mode we easily steamrollered through much of the game in one evening, pausing to catch our breath and realising we were only a stone's throw from the final boss. The problems begin with the design of the levels. While they do challenge you from time to time, and gathering all the treasure will keep you busy, the vast majority yielded 100 per cent of their wares to us on the first go. Only a fraction of them needed us to run through them more than once or twice to obtain everything, and even the bosses rarely took more than a couple of tries. Even if your mileage does vary, surely it won't by the sort of margin required to stretch Kururin Squash out over more than a Sunday afternoon.

Ironically, as much as we owe this failing to lenient level design, superior controls are also to blame. The digital response of the GBA titles often made it harder, but the analogue control here is deadly smooth. The stick goes precisely where you want it to go and allows for much finer control through tricky situations, while the levels don't clamp down on you to compensate.

We also feel that it was slightly misguided to flesh it all out with the racing mode bit, even if it has worked before. It's more Time Trial in its approach than anything else, with levels unlocked more or less from the get-go, and arguably could have done with losing the checkpoints to up the ante and giving us multiple, staggered goal times to aspire to instead. We would have preferred twice as many regular puzzle levels to this against-the-clock stuff, really, and as a multiplayer mode it only works when all the players are at a similar skill level. Admittedly getting to a similar level isn't massively difficult, but how likely is it as a regular pick-up game with that in mind? And, while we're on the attack, we never did shake the feeling that, while attempts to break free of the central spinny evasion idea are admirable, they never really do as much for us as the pure alternative.

Finally the deathmatch mode. Initially we thought it was a bit unbalanced. It does, after all, combine a number of power-ups that were designed for the single-player game and then thrown together without warning. But in time it reveals itself to be a more Monkey Target-esque luck of the draw scenario, and with four players it can be manic. It's got a certain charm about it, that's for sure. But as for whether it's manic enough to displace the likes of Monkey Ball and Mario Kart in the grand scheme of Cube party pieces, we have our doubts. More likely it's half an hour's entertainment halfway through an evening in with your mates.

Contorted
---------

The net result of which is that you'll have tremendous fun playing Kururin Squash while it lasts, but that for all its improvements and clever ideas it's let down by an unfortunate shortfall in the quantity and quality of its levels. It just doesn't push you hard enough or for long enough, and the extras (also including a throwaway downloadable GBA mini-game) don't add much. In the end it's not worth what it'll probably cost you to import (despite its budget price point in Japan, you're bound to encounter import mark-up), and while we'd dearly love to see things like this cross the void between Japan and the West, it's hard to recommend this one particularly. If you've not played Kururin before, you should, but unless you haven't got a Game Boy you should look for Kuru Kuru Kururin or the Japanese sequel Kururin Paradise on eBay instead.

That said, if you are a Kururin vet and happen to stumble across Squash for £16 while trawling importers on a darkening afternoon in Soho as we did, it's an evening of all the beautiful, quirkily executed ideas from which are modern story-driven third-person action-blockbuster wotsits were originally derived, calling for speedy reactions and a touch of lateral thinking, and you will have fun. Just not enough of it. In other words, it'll captivate you for as long as it lasts, but don't be surprised if it then spins off onto a shelf with only a duck in a helicopter's chance of ever returning to the fore.

[Shop for games now with Simply Games.](http://www.simplygames.com/index.asp?aid=1000)

7 / 10

Small(ish) library, BIG surprises!

*   ![Image 15: Kimimi](https://images.nintendolife.com/users/85543/avatar.jpg?v=1386763281)

_Image: Zion Grassl / Nintendo Life_

The North American 20th anniversary of Nintendo's cube-y console is upon us and we’ve come to realise that two entire decades is long enough for people to either [forget the GameCube’s charming boxy shape](https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2021/11/random-oh-no-people-dont-recognise-gamecubes-any-more) or even grow to adulthood without ever handling Nintendo’s handled hardware. "0 years is also plenty of time for anything less than the very best and brightest examples of the system’s library to quietly fade from memory.

*   [**Best GameCube Games**](https://www.nintendolife.com/guides/50-best-gamecube-games-of-all-time)

Subscribe to [Nintendo Life](https://www.youtube.com/nintendolife?sub_confirmation=1) on [YouTube 841k](https://www.youtube.com/nintendolife?sub_confirmation=1)

So while this is the perfect time to dust off much-loved copies of [F-Zero GX](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/f-zero_gx), [Super Smash Bros.](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/super_smash_bros_melee)[Melee](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/super_smash_bros_melee), and [Metroid Prime](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/metroid_prime) for one more happy go, why don’t we dig a little deeper and celebrate the console’s wider and more unusual releases as well? Here we pick out some slightly more obscure imports and curios that often get barged out of the spotlight by [Wind Waker](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/legend_of_zelda_the_wind_waker), [RE4](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/resident_evil_4) and the rest...

[Kururin Squash! (GCN)](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/kururin_squash)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 17: Kururin Squash! (GCN)](https://images.nintendolife.com/78c34bd7689ef/kururin-squash-artwork.900x250.jpg)

[![Image 18: Kururin Squash! (GCN)](https://images.nintendolife.com/dda4c24ff6410/kururin-squash-cover.cover_small.jpg)](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/kururin_squash)

*   [7.0](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/kururin_squash "Based on 19 user ratings")
*   [Profile](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/kururin_squash)

Publisher: **Nintendo** / Developer: **Eighting**

Release Date: **14th Oct 2004 (JPN)**

“More [Kururin](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gba/kuru_kuru_kururin)” is really all the description this game needs — who doesn’t want to play more Kururin?

The simple-to-grasp yet difficult-to-master wall-avoiding gameplay that made the launch GBA title such an unexpected highlight is present and correct here, the all-new 3D surroundings sensibly used to lightly enhance rather than over-complicate the already perfect formula. Sadly this title turned out to be the final outing for Nintendo’s whirly action-puzzle series, but at least it went out on a high.

*   [Review 7/10](https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/2009/04/odama_retro)
*   [Profile](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/odama)

Publisher: **Nintendo** / Developer: **Vivarium**

Release Date: **10th Apr 2006 (USA)** / **31st Mar 2006 (UK/EU)**

Somehow this imaginative mix of pinball and feudal Japanese warring got a worldwide release, and we’re very glad it did. Use giant flippers to propel the titular ball towards your enemies, order your troops via the oft-forgotten GameCube microphone, and do your very best to get your bell to the goal in time.

Part-arcade action, part-tactics, part-shouting, [Odama](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/odama) won't be everyone's idea of a must-have title, but then again we’d hope for nothing less unusual from the mind responsible for the Dreamcast’s most famous talking fish, **Seaman**.

Publisher: **Nintendo** / Developer: **Nintendo**

Release Date: **20th Sep 2002 (UK/EU)**

[Doshin the Giant](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/doshin_the_giant) debuted on Nintendo’s expensive and exclusively Japanese 64DD add-on, although this European-released port of the giant’s island-based shenanigans is thankfully slightly easier to get hold of.

Reminiscent of [Populous](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gameboy/populous) before it and **[From Dust](http://www.pushsquare.com/games/ps3/from_dust)** after it, the aim is to use your god-like powers to raise and lower the terrain to better suit your island’s inhabitants and generally help them out, which in turn will result in them loving (or hating) your giant yellow form.

Publisher: **Atlus** / Developer: **Intelligent Systems**

Release Date: **5th Nov 2002 (USA)**

Another project initially imagined for Nintendo’s Japanese N64 disc drive, although this one has the distinction of never releasing on that earlier rewritable format. The striking low-poly visuals used to navigate the blocky [Cubivore](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/cubivore_survival_of_the_fittest) world help to abstract an experience that routinely asks you to not only defeat your enemies, but _tear them limb from limb_ before consuming their bodies, all in a bid to mutate, mate, and be reborn into a form capable of overthrowing the Killer Cubivore.

Publisher: **Hudson Soft** / Developer: **Red Entertainment**

Release Date: **18th Dec 2003 (JPN)**

[Smash Bros](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/nintendo-switch/super_smash_bros_ultimate) may now have excellent versions of two of the most popular Belmonts, as well as a huge quantity of fantastic remixes of classic **[Castlevania](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/nes/castlevania)** tracks to go with them, but there’s still only one crossover fighting game that lets legendary vampire killer Simon take on [**Transformers**](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/wiiu/transformers_prime)' Optimus Prime _._

It’s fair to say nothing’s ever going to beat Sakurai’s series when it comes to crossovers, but Konami’s attempt to take the genre throne is at the very least a colourful jumble of recognisable faces and grin-inducing ‘_Wait, they really included that guy?!_’ character choices.

[P.N.03 (GCN)](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/p_n_03)
------------------------------------------------------------------

Publisher: **Nintendo** / Developer: **Capcom Production Studio 4**

Release Date: **9th Sep 2003 (USA)** / **29th Aug 2003 (UK/EU)**

AKA: 'That time Shinji Mikami, forever most famous for giving the world the survival horror masterpiece **[Resident Evil](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/resident_evil)**, decided he wanted to create an intense and deeply stylish action game'.

One of the infamous 'Capcom Five', [P.N.03](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/p.n.03) features distinct enemy types that work together within tightly controlled arenas to make each room its own mesmerising score attack action-puzzle sequence; and with a little practice players will find themselves executing perfectly timed balletic twirls straight _through_ incoming laser fire, all the while enveloped by the clean lines and smooth curves of unmistakably Y2K-style architecture.

[Lost Kingdoms (GCN)](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/lost_kingdoms)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 29: Lost Kingdoms (GCN)](https://images.nintendolife.com/d3863a178d7eb/lost-kingdoms-artwork.900x250.jpg)

[![Image 30: Lost Kingdoms (GCN)](https://images.nintendolife.com/f33fd414ed94b/lost-kingdoms-cover.cover_small.jpg)](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/lost_kingdoms)

*   [Profile](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/lost_kingdoms)

Publisher: **Activision** / Developer: **FromSoftware**

Release Date: **27th May 2002 (USA)** / **9th Aug 2002 (UK/EU)**

Combine the depth of an RPG with the irresistible nature of card collecting, add a dash of action and you’ve got GameCube exclusive [Lost Kingdoms](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/lost_kingdoms), a dark adventure from a quirky little developer called FromSoftware. [_Whatever happened to them?_](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/nintendo-switch/dark_souls_remastered)

In yet another twist away from RPG norms, the heroine, Katia, never attacks directly herself and is instead entirely reliant on the monsters she summons forth from the cards she buys, captures, and transforms, with players aiming to build a deck capable of taking on the mysterious entity behind the deadly Black Fog.

Publisher: **Nintendo** / Developer: **Intelligent Systems**

Release Date: **7th Feb 2003 (JPN)**

Far more than a repackaged bundle of previously released classics (not that we ever mind seeing games this good make a comeback), this tricky trio of Nintendo-born puzzlers — that’s **[Panel de Pon](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/snes/tetris_attack)**, **[Dr. Mario 64](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/nes/dr_mario)**, and **[Yoshi’s Cookie](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/nes/yoshis_cookie)** — contained on one convenient disc look and play better than ever before.

Whichever title’s your personal favourite, you can look forward to competitive matches against up to four players as well as the chance to take the game on the portable; just connect a GBA to the console and download the original release of these evergreen brain-teasers (and don't turn the power off until you're done).

Publisher: **Nintendo** / Developer: **Nintendo EAD**

Release Date: **7th Jun 2004 (USA)** / **7th Jan 2005 (UK/EU)**

‘_What if The Legend of Zelda, a series famous since the ‘80’s for its fiendish puzzles and absorbing dungeon-based solo gameplay, suddenly became a frantic cooperative riot?_’ asks [Four Swords Adventures](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/gamecube/legend_of_zelda_four_swords_adventures) — and the only answer possible is: ‘_It’d be a heck of a lot of fun_’.

With an enjoyably episodic adventure at its heart, a competitive mode for those times you want to unleash Link’s familiar arsenal against your friends, and a beautiful ‘SNES+’ graphical style, there’s plenty of reasons to keep your SP fully charged and, even when playing alone, there's a lot to love. It’s never been easy (or cheap) to set up the quantity of handhelds and cables necessary to play it with a full group of people, but it’s always been worth the effort.

Publisher: **Nintendo** / Developer: **Nintendo EAD**

Release Date: **14th Mar 2005 (USA)** / **4th Feb 2005 (UK/EU)**

Guide the first member of the DK Crew to banana-collecting victory in this accessible platformer that uses the most unusual control scheme of them all — _bongos_. That’s right! Grab your plastic percussion and tap, slap, and clap your way through 16 worlds of fruit-themed adventure.

A muscular monkey’s mightiest moment? Maybe not, but the team that made this went on to make [Super Mario Galaxy](https://www.nintendolife.com/games/wii/super_mario_galaxy), which should tell you something. If you’re tired of bringing out the same old rhythm games at parties, this makes for an ape-tacular alternative.

**Sonic****Riders** is the best racing game I've ever played, it's extremely satisfying once you understand most of the rules. And the character selection is quite generous.

**Zatch****Bell****Mamodo Fury** is an interesting hybrid action/fighting game where you exchange blows from far away. It's not incredibly deep but gets quite challenging to A rank all stages. And once again unlocking the characters is pretty fun (20 playable characters)

Despite my love for GC I don't really have a lot of games I could call overlooked. So might as well: **Shadow****the****Hedgehog** gameplay-wise a stepdown from the highly technical gameplay from the previous game, it still manages to be fun, as most levels are plenty filled with 3D action and platforming and performs great on GameCube. It's pretty brutal if you go for all A ranks and endings. But you're awarded with an Expert Mode that is basically a linear, perfected version of the game.
